items.stem: The polynomial $f(x) = 9x^{3} - x^{4} + 2$ has its terms written out of order. Which statement describes the end behavior of its graph?
items.hint: Only the term of highest degree decides both ends, and it is not always the term written first.
worked: The degrees present are $3$, $4$ and $0$, so the leading term is $-x^{4}$, not $9x^{3}$.
The degree $4$ is even, so both ends of the graph travel in the same direction.
The leading coefficient is $-1$, which is negative, so that shared direction is downward.

options.text: $f(x) \to 0$ as $x \to -\infty$ and $f(x) \to 0$ as $x \to +\infty$, so the graph levels off toward $y = 0$

items.stem: Exactly one of the four polynomials below has a graph that rises on both ends, meaning $f(x) \to +\infty$ as $x \to -\infty$ and also $f(x) \to +\infty$ as $x \to +\infty$. Which one is it?
items.hint: Rewrite each choice until you can read off a single highest-power term, then ask whether that power is even and whether the number in front of it is positive.
worked: Both ends rise only when the degree is even AND the leading coefficient is positive.
$5x^{3} - x^{4}$ has leading term $-x^{4}$: even degree but a negative coefficient, so both ends fall.
$x^{2}(x^{3}+1) = x^{5} + x^{2}$ has degree $2 + 3 = 5$, and $(x^{3})^{3} = x^{3 \cdot 3} = x^{9}$ has degree $9$; both degrees are odd, so those ends go opposite ways.
$x^{4} + 6x^{3}$ has leading term $x^{4}$: even degree, positive coefficient, so both ends rise.

items.stem: A student is asked for the end behavior of $p(x) = -2x^{3}(x^{2} + 7)$ and writes: 'the leading term is $-2x^{6}$, the degree is even, so the graph falls on both ends.' Which choice identifies the mistake and gives the correct end behavior?
items.hint: The leading term of a product is the product of the leading terms; check what multiplying like bases does to their exponents.
worked: The leading term of $p$ comes from $(-2x^{3})(x^{2})$.
Multiplying like bases adds the exponents: $-2x^{3+2} = -2x^{5}$. The student multiplied $3 \cdot 2$ instead and got $x^{6}$.
Degree $5$ is odd and the leading coefficient $-2$ is negative, so the two ends go opposite ways.
As $x \to -\infty$, $p(x) \to +\infty$; as $x \to +\infty$, $p(x) \to -\infty$. The graph rises on the left and falls on the right.

options.text: There is no mistake: the leading term is $-2x^{6}$, so the graph falls on both ends.
The degree $6$ is right; the mistake is the sign, because $-2x^{6}$ comes out positive for every nonzero $x$, so the graph rises on both ends.
Exponents add when like bases multiply, so the leading term is $-2x^{5}$; an odd degree with a negative coefficient means the graph rises on the left and falls on the right.
The leading term is $-2x^{5}$, so the degree is odd and the graph falls on the left and rises on the right.
